text: This expression hides a double meaning, as the word "mesiats" may mean both "moon" and "month." The author is at once suggesting that "the month is clear" (a rather indeterminate time setting) and that "the moon shines." The formulation recalls also Nikolai Gogol's *Diary of a Madman* (1834): "I don't remember the date. There was also no month" (Ostanin 10). Finally, this opening sets up the novel's fixation on seasonal time markers, as opposed to those created by humans.

В первом случае это довольно неопределенное указание на время года, а во втором случае описывается, как луна сияет на небе. Формулировка напоминает "Записки сумасшедшего" Н. Гоголя: "Числа не помню. Месяца тоже не было" (Останин 10). К тому же, такое начало книги подсказывает, что в романе время движется согласно природным знакам времен года, оно не измеряется человеческими инструментами, приборами.

text: Elena Kravchenko writes: "Sokolov differs from both the avant-garde aestheticization of the real and the conceptualist disclosure of the hyper-real. Firstly, reality is a priori presented in a reflected form through a series of artistic representations. Secondly, in his engagement with these signs, Sokolov does not simply abstract them from their 'original' function or context, but grounds them in their original medium: language. [...]. A pun, produced through a play on the homonym 'mesiats', throws off the reader, forcing him to reflect on the plurality of signifieds covered by a single name. By using the adjective 'iasnyi' (clear), with its indication of both clarity as colour and a level of intelligibility, the narrator provokes a double entendre, thus revealing the basis of the notion of time: the abstract category of time is grounded in a spatial (alberit heavenly) body" (*The Prose* 71).
ru_trans: Елена Кравченко пишет: "Соколов отличается как от авангардной эстетизации реального, так и от концептуалистического раскрытия гиперреального. Во-первых, реальность априори представлена ​​в отраженной форме через ряд художественных изображений. Во-вторых, в своем взаимодействии с этими символами Соколов не просто абстрагирует их от их "исходной" функции или контекста, но обосновывает их в их изначальной среде: языке. […]. Каламбур, произведенный посредством игры с омонимом "месяц", сбивает читателя с толку, заставляя его размышлять о множественности охватываемых одним именем символов. Используя прилагательное "ясный" с его указанием как на выразительность цвета, так и на уровень понятности, рассказчик провоцирует двусмысленность, тем самым раскрывая основу понятия времени: абстрактная категория времени обосновывается в пространственном (хотя и небесном) теле" (Kravchenko, "The Prose" 71).

text: Sokolov once described the process of writing *Between Dog and Wolf* as follows: "because I had little time, I wrote, primarily, poems. I couldn't write prose. It requires a long 'entrance.' It simply requires continues life, somehow constant. But you can write poets in a train, anywhere you want ... And therefore I also wrote a lot of poems for this book in Switzerland. And in Austria. In Austria I could write every evening but poems. Because when you return home from the forest at nine with axe, with a pitchfork or a saw in your hands, there's simply no talk about prose. Therefore, that's probably *Sobaka's* form is so unusual, why poems and prose are interspersed" (Polovets 8).

text: Galoshes. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.
ru_trans: Резиновая обувь. Д. Б. Джонсон отмечает более двадцати видов обуви, встречающихся в трех романах Соколова: “башмаки, ботфорты, боты, ботинки (полуботинки), чеботы, чизмы, чубуры, галоши (калоши), геты, ичиги, кеды, клоги, лапти, мокроступы, обуви (обувки), сапоги, сандалии, тапочки (полутапочки), шлепанцы, штиблеты, тапти, туфли, валенки. Список можно расширить, включив такие атрибуты, как носки, чулки, портянки, гамаши, коньки, костыли и протезы” (Johnson, “The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Что касается “Между собакой и волком”, он замечает, что фамилия Ильи сразу наталкивает на мысль о хрустальных туфельках Золушки. Джонсон подчеркивает, что “мотив обуви — дань Соколова, будь то осознанная или неосознанная, традициям русской литературы, представленным его предшественниками — И. Буниным и В. Катаевым” (179). В интервью с А. и Н. Воронелями, Соколов называет Бунина и Гоголя своими “современниками, сотрудниками по цеху, старшими мастерами” (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Мотив обуви.

text: Allusion to the author’s biography and to the situation many authors were facing in the 1980s. It is also relevant that Sokolov uses the word 'priiateli' (echoed also in the adj. druzhesky in the reference from the *Evgeny Onegin*): when in dispersion (i.e., exile), people who belong to the other (non-official / "second") culture can rebuild the links among them.

text: Interestingly enough, Sokolov avoids using the most common Soviet appellative "Tovarishch" opting for a rather general, but still evocative word (think of Nikolay Nekrasov's "Poet i grazhdanin," Poet and Citizen, 1856). The choice could be also related to the epistolary genre Ilya is here trying to reproduce and to the fact that this world is rather the 'old' term substituting the Soviet “Tovarishch.”
ru_trans: Интерено отметить, что Соколов избегает употребления советского обращения "товарищ", предпочитая ему более общий, но все еще значимый термин (ср. Н. А. Некрасов "Поэт и гражданин", 1856). Выбор может также подсказывать, что Илья намерен писать заявление "правильно" и думает выражениями, типичными для "старого" (несоветского или, скорее, досоветского) времени.

text: Sidor (shortened form of Isidor), son of Foma. Here the declension of the name is incorrect (should be in the dative case, Sidoru). In colloquial language, the names are sometimes declined incorrectly for easier pronunciation: Сан Санычу (San Sanychu), Михал Валерьичу (Mikhal Valer'ichu), etc. The name Isidor (or Sidor) originally means "son or gift of Isis," the major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion, an ideal of femininity and motherhood who was also believed to help the dead enter the afterlife.

В разговорной речи, имена иногда склоняются не совсем верно для более удобного произношения: Сан Санычу, Михал Валерьичу, и т. п. An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As M. Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*); in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: Sokolov comments: "You may have noticed that cats, while strolling in the garden or in the woods, find some nice-tasting grasses and chew them. Specialists say that cats do this instinctively: those grasses are healing. Humans, though perhaps not all, have the same instinct. In our childhood and adolescence, it is evident. Once in nature, a child strives to pick up a leaf of grass or a tree and chew it, this action is involuntary. In adolescence and later we do it less often, but we cannot completely get rid of the habit of chewing something. If there is no plant at hand, we chew a pencil, a paintbrush, a pen. This helps creativity, becomes an integral part of it. Chewing or munching something, we involuntarily masticate, i.e. salivate this object. Alas, it is not quite aesthetic, but we cannot change this state of affairs. The phrase 'to soil the dark-green leaf' contains no hint of something more complicated; it is merely a glimpse, a small aspect of a specific past" (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

Специалисты говорят, что кошки поступают так инстинктивно: те травинки целебны. Людям, пусть, может быть, и не всем, присущ тот же инстинкт. В нашем детстве и отрочестве он проявляется со всей очевидностью. Оказавшись на природе, ребенок норовит сорвать лист травы или дерева и пожевать его, это действие безотчетно. В юности и позже мы делаем это реже, но полностью изжить в себе привычку что-нибудь пожевать не удается. Если под рукой нет растения, грызем карандаш, кисть, перо. Это помогает творчеству,  становится его неотъемлемой частью. Грызя или жуя что-либо, мы невольно мусолим, то есть слюнявим данный предмет. Увы, это не вполне эстетично, но изменить такое вот положение дел мы не в силах. Фраза 'мусолить жирно-зеленый лист' не содержит намека на нечто более сложное, это просто промельк, малый аспект конкретного прошлого" (личная переписка, 7 июня 2023).

Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: Burdock. Plant motif. This word is also used to describe a loser, a misfortune, silly, or weak person who "flaps their ears like a burdock at their happiness." Here, this word follows “тупик” (и в тупике, где лопух) — “a dead end” (both literal (e. g., a wall) and metaphorical (a hopeless situation)) — but it also shares the same root with a very common insult “тупой" (a stupid person).
ru_trans: Мотив растений. В разговорной речи "лопух" также определяет неудачника, слабого и глуповатого человека, который "прохлопал ушами (как лопухом) своё счастье". В предложении этому слову предшествует существительное "тупик" ("и в тупике, где лопух") — отсутствие выхода (и буквально (непроходимый конец улицы), и метафорически (безнадежная ситуация)), — которое разделяет один и тот же корень с оскорбительной характеристикой "тупой" (глупый человек).

Double meaning, very relevant from a thematic point of view for the plot: okhota = 1. hunting / 2. desire.
The quote is from B. Pasternak, *Doctor Zhivago*, part 5, chapter 14.
It is also interesting to notice that in Pasternak's novel this “young man” is the interlocutor with whom Zhivago converses while on the train: "Once in the dark of the night, the interlocutor turns out to be deaf and, therefore, capable of sustaining a conversation solely by lip reading. This pivotal sequence in Pasternak’s novel unravels the theme of incommunicability, a topic that is of great interest to Sokolov too. By evoking the idea of the power of language and of its sound, which not everyone is capable of hearing, Sokolov once again stresses the redeeming sacredness of the word. After all, this seemingly epistolary second novel by Sokolov presents itself as a letter addressed to detective Pozhilykh by Ilya Zynzyrela (later discovered to be dead), in which the sender seeks justice for a wrongdoing. Thus, the writing offers a refuge and a redemption from (linear) time and death" (Napolitano, *Sasha Sokolov* 88).
Elena Kravchenko also writes, "The unsettling feeling, triggered by the man's intense gaze, overly articulate speech, and lapses into occasional withdrawals, is explained next day. He is deaf, and in order to hear and therefore speak, he needs to see and read the lips of his collocutor. By virtue of his link with Pasternak's hunter, Iakov can be associated with the visual aspect of language. It is also reflected in his artistic aspirations, manifested in the 'picture gallery' of the prose section" (*Reflections* 81).

Кравченко также пишет: "Тревожное чувство, вызванное пристальным взглядом мужчины, чрезмерно членораздельной речью и периодическими отстранениями, объясняется на следующий день. Благодаря своей схожести с охотником Пастернака, Якова можно связать с визуальным аспектом языка. Это также отражено в его художественных стремлениях, проявленных в "картинках с выставки" прозаической части" ((Kravchenko, "Reflections" 81)).

text: Another name given to Orina, the central female figure in the novel. In the chapters devoted to Yakov, she becomes his mother, thus the characters enact a variation on the Oedipal myth. Hanna Kolb writes: "She is a *Rossiia-mater'* (little mother Russia) (65) in eighteenth-century language [...] She is the Volga, the wolf-river which gives them crayfish to eat and water to drink, a stone under their heads, but also a stone around their necks. In each of the only two women's names that occur in the text, Orina and Mariia, may be heard "*rodina*" (native land), as well as "*mat'* (mother). Mariia is Iyakov's mother and the mother of God, about whom Il'a [sic] speaks in his Christmas sermon [...], both a mother goddess and the Mother of God. The lover Orina is raised in the figure of the Lady to sainthood, to the role of Blok's simultaneously life-giving [...] and death-giving "*neponiatnaia neznakomka*" (115)" (204). Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Colloquial: gimp, stump. See also Bruegel's painting *The Beggars* (1568): *Beggars* touches on a number of Sokolovian themes: deformities and handicaps, dancing, inversions of social order. It likewise features the fox imagery of *Between Dog and Wolf*. Manfred Sellink writes, “these paupers are performing (or rather trying to perform) a dance. The man in the centre, looking out at us, has straps with bells around his legs. The faces that can be seen have their mouths open, as it they are singing. The cripples are all dressed up, their white garments with foxtails mockingly evoking […] the expensive ermine robes worn by the most rich and powerful. This suggestion is strengthened by their equally evident headdresses, mimicking those on the heads of the mighty: a mitre, a crown and a fur cap. Given the fact that Bruegel is working here on a motif from his earlier Carnival painting, the painting touches on one of the essential aspects of Carnival festivities - a moment that briefly reverses the normal social order and class distinctions […] The appearance of the foxtails in conjunction with beggars in two totally different paintings, one dating from 1559 and the other from 1568, suggests that here the attribute is associated with popular customs, possibly connected with Carnival and Shrove Tuesday. There were longstanding traditions in which foxtails were seen as symbols of foolishness and deceit” (283).
ru_trans: Разговорное: калека, инвалид. См. также картину Брейгеля "Калеки" (1568). "Калеки" затрагивают ряд соколовских тем: уродство, калечество, танцы, инверсия социального порядка. В ней также присутствует образ лисы из "Между собакой и волком". М. Селлинк пишет: "Эти калеки исполняют (или, скорее, пытаются исполнить) танец. У человека в центре, смотрящего на нас, на ногах ремни с колокольчиками. Лица, которые можно увидеть, открывают рты, как будто они поют. Калеки все разодеты, их белые одежды с лисьими хвостами насмешливо вызывают в памяти […] дорогие горностаевые мантии, которые носят самые богатые и могущественные. Это предположение усиливается их столь же очевидными головными уборами, имитирующими те, что на головах могущественных людей: митра, корона и меховая шапка. Учитывая тот факт, что Брейгель работает здесь над мотивом из своей более ранней картины "Битва Масленицы и Поста", картина затрагивает один из существенных аспектов карнавальных празднеств — момент, который на короткое время меняет обычный социальный порядок и классовые различия […] Появление лисьих хвостов в сочетании с нищими на двух совершенно разных картинах, одна из которых датируется 1559 годом, а другая — 1568 годом, предполагает, что здесь этот атрибут связан с народными обычаями, возможно, связанными с Карнавалом и Масленицей. Существовали давние традиции, в которых лисьи хвосты рассматривались как символы глупости и обмана" (Sellink 283).

text: Braid, scythe, or sandback/spit. The ambiguity of the word “kosa” has a famous literary “predecessor” in Aleksandr Blok’s drama *Balaganchik* (*The Puppet Show*, 1906). The female character of Columbine has a “kosa” behind her back: either a hair braid or a scythe. The “mystics” warn Pierrot about her being Death, but he calls her his bride (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”; I don't listen to fairy tales. I am a simple man. You will not deceive me. This is Columbine. This is my bride). The ambiguity is also stressed by the character of the Author who enters the scene and exclaims: “Я не признаю [...] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” (I do not recognize [...] such allegorical wordplay: it is indecent to call a woman's braid a scythe of death! It denigrates a lady's status!). In the end, Pierrot sadly discovers that this Columbine was just a “cardboard bride” (Она картонной невестой была). The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). Read the original by Blok [here](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B8%D0%BA_(%D0%91%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%BA)).
ru_trans: Плетеная коса (прическа), серп (жнеца смерти) или речная коса. Неоднозначность слова "коса" предшествуется драмой А. А. Блока "Балаганчик" ("Шоу марионеток" 1906). У героини по имени Колумбина есть "коса" за спиной: это или плетеные волосы, или же серп. "Мистики" предупреждают Пьера о том, что Колумбина есть Смерть, но от отрицает это, называя её свой невестой (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”). Неоднозначность усиливается, когда герой Автора вторгается в сцену и восклицает: Я не признаю […] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” В конце Пьер с горестью обнаруживает, что всё это время Колубмина была "картонной невестой". Ключевая тема, связывающая женскую любовь со смертью, проводит параллель между соколовским романом и блоковским "Балаганчиком", хоть она и разрабатывалась продолжительной литературной традицией в течение очень долгого времени (например, Эрос и Танатос, "Ненавижу и люблю" Катулла). Прочитать драму Блока можно [по ссылке](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Балаганчик_(Блок)).

text: Another name given to Orina, the central female figure in the novel. In the chapters devoted to Yakov, she becomes his mother, thus the characters enact a variation on the Oedipal myth. Hanna Kolb writes: "She is a *Rossiia-mater*' (little mother Russia) (65) in eighteenth-century language […] She is the Volga, the wolf-river which gives them crayfish to eat and water to drink, a stone under their heads, but also a stone around their necks. In each of the only two women's names that occur in the text, Orina and Mariia, may be heard "*rodina*" (native land), as well as "*mat*'" (mother). Mariia is Iyakov's mother and the mother of God, about whom Il'a [sic] speaks in his Christmas sermon […], both a mother goddess and the Mother of God. The lover Orina is raised in the figure of the Lady to sainthood, to the role of Blok's simultaneously life-giving […] and death-giving "*neponiatnaia neznakomka*" (115)" (204). Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Дедушкин табак (grandfather's tobacco) is another name for the lycoperdon genus of mostly edible puffball mushrooms. Прочитать больше можно [здесь](https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/a-puff-of-wolf-flatulence-9mt7wmp3n) (статья на английском) или [здесь](https://ria.ru/20220523/dozhdevik-1790157119.html?ysclid=la3dvo9o2k862304870) (статья на русском). The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). text: This verb both introduces the bird motif, associating characters with birds (and, more generally, animals), and suggests via its figurative meaning ("being forced to be somewhere") the itinerant nature of Ilya. José Vergara suggests that Sokolov's bird imagery "underscores the inherent tie between the characters (humanity) and nature in the novel. That is, the natural world in the guise of various animals does not only reflect the characters’ emotions and experiences. They may wish to overcome their status as beings of flesh, blood, and nature, but the bird imagery – among other things – constantly reminds them of their earthbound existence. They seek to escape the pull of the mundane and wearisome existence they live and to reach an ideal, but they are consistently dragged back down" ("Flap" 364).
ru_trans: Данный глагол и вводит "птичий мотив", связывая персонажей и птиц (или вообще животных), и образно подсказывает передвижной и странствующий характер Ильи. Хосе Вергара считает, что птичья тематика Соколова "подчеркивает присущую роману связь между персонажами (человечеством) и природой". То есть мир природы в облике различных животных не только отражает эмоции и переживания персонажей. Они могут хотеть преодолеть свой статус существ из плоти, крови и природы, но образы птиц — помимо всего прочего — постоянно напоминают им об их земном существовании. Они стремятся освободиться от притяжения обыденного и утомительного существования, которым они живут, и достичь идеала, но их постоянно тянет обратно вниз" ("Flap" 364).

text: The workers' cooperative (a joint venture) is in contrast with the "individuals" who work there. This pairing, in a sense, describes the novel's use of "forking characters" who constantly shift names and identities. For this reason, *Between Dog and Wolf* has often, though too simplistically been called the "Russian *Finnegans Wake*. For example, Richard Borden writes, "Aside from its perceived inaccessibility, its extremely disjointed narrative, its profound elusiveness and allusiveness, the fundamental timelessness of its narrative, its seeming to operate more according to the laws of dream than of waking experience, its wealth of neologism and, in particular, of complex paronomasia, *Between Dog and Wolf* resembles *Finnegans Wake* in its forking characters, in the way characters seem to dissolve one into the other—or evolve one from the other" ("Toward" 389).

По этой причине "Между собакой и волком" часто, хотя и чересчур упрощенно, называли "русскими 'Поминками по Финнегану'". Например, Р. text: This name is linked with the Old East Slavic text "Praying (or Supplication) of Daniil Zatochnik" (13th century), addressed to the Prince of Pereyaslavl and Suzdal in order to receive help and grace. In addition to "sharpen," the root verb in the name Zatochnik, zatochnit', also means to "imprison" (so Daniil could have been an exiled man). Thus, there is an irony with what Ilya writes about never having been incarcerated. D. Zatochnik is echoed also in Sokolov's *A School for Fools*, when the main character describes his fictional work at his father's office as being a "pencil sharpener": "Первое время мы служили в прокуратуре у отца, он взял нас к себе на должность точильщиков карандашей, и мы побывали на многих судебных заседаниях" (in English, the translation is slightly different: "At first we worked for our father in the prosecutor's office; he hired us as filers of files and we were present at many court proceedings") (E174/R143).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

text: The workers' cooperative (a joint venture) is in contrast with the "individuals" who work there. This pairing, in a sense, describes the novel's use of "forking characters" who constantly shift names and identities. For this reason, *Between Dog and Wolf* has often, though too simplistically been called the "Russian *Finnegans Wake*. For example, Richard Borden writes, "Aside from its perceived inaccessibility, its extremely disjointed narrative, its profound elusiveness and allusiveness, the fundamental timelessness of its narrative, its seeming to operate more according to the laws of dream than of waking experience, its wealth of neologism and, in particular, of complex paronomasia, *Between Dog and Wolf* resembles *Finnegans Wake* in its forking characters, in the way characters seem to dissolve one into the other—or evolve one from the other" ("Toward" 389).

text: In the original: D. Zatochnik. This name is linked with the Old East Slavic text "Praying (or Supplication) of Daniil Zatochnik" (13th century), addressed to the Prince of Pereyaslavl and Suzdal in order to receive help and grace. In addition to "sharpen," the root verb in the name Zatochnik, zatochnit', also means to "imprison" (so Daniil could have been an exiled man). Thus, there is an irony with what Ilya writes about never having been incarcerated. Boguslawski approximates this play on Zatochnik's name by referencing Schopenhauer. D. Zatochnik is echoed also in Sokolov's *A School for Fools*, when the main character describes his fictional work at his father's office as being a "pencil sharpener": "At first we worked for our father in the prosecutor's office; he hired us as filers of files and we were present at many court proceedings" (R143/E174).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Galoshes. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text:
Sokolov explains: "That of the coupler is a very dangerous profession. In those years, desperate and degraded people joined the couplers, many of them had a criminal record, some had been in jail for long. The time in prison undermined their health and, in particular, ruined their teeth. When released from prison, they had them repaired and covered by metal crowns.
Many convicts had crowns on many teeth, but among serious thieves and criminals it was fashionable to have just one gold tooth. The gold-toothed couplers were treated with special respect and caution. At the beginning of her career Maria's lovers were these gold-toothed couplers, that is, guys with a criminal bent, but when she became a supervisor, higher-ranking men began to approach her - machinists" (personal communication, June 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "Сцепщик - профессия весьма опасная. В сцепщики в оные годы шли люди отчаянные и деклассированные, многие из них с криминальным прошлым, отсидевшие серьезные сроки. Сроки эти подорвали их здоровье, в частности, испортили им зубы. Выйдя на свободу, они чинили их, ставили металлические коронки. У многих сидельцев коронки были на многих зубах, но среди серьезных воров и бандитов модно было иметь фиксу лишь на одном зубе. К фиксатым относились с особым уважением и робостью. В начале ее карьеры любовники Марии были те самые фиксатые, то есть ребята с уголовным уклоном, а когда она стала начальницей, к ней стали приходить ухажеры более высокого ранга - машинисты" (личное сообщение, 7 июня 2023).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. text: Метель (blizzard) was previously spelled мятель, as заяц (hare) was once spelled заец. In this section, as Martina Napolitano suggests, Sokolov plays with "the close pronunciation of certain unaccented vowels in Russian, which often gives rise to misspelling – я, е, й" (“Studyin This Volapuke” 289). Letters are transferred from word/concept to word/concept. The pairs metel'/miatel' and zaits/zaets appear in connection with different linguistic phenomena: metel'/miatel' reflects an alternative use of the vowel linked to the spelling instability still dominant in the nineteenth century and on which many authors, from Pushkin to Blok, played, also because of the possibility to reflect a different semantic intention (see Vasil'ev). Metel', in fact, has its root in the verb mesti, to sweep, while that of miatel' is to be found in the verb miastis', to provoke smiatenie (confusion, disarray); in authors who make conscious and calibrated use of the two variants, it is precisely with this condition that the use of miatel' is to be associated, as its strong expressive connotation prevails over the simple and objective identification of the natural phenomenon. Zaiats-zaets refers to the different outcome of the nasalised -e- of late proto-Slavic, which becomes, in East Slavonic, -ia- and, in South Slavonic, -e-: zaiats is, therefore, the more purely Russian form, while zaets reflects Slavonic-ecclesiastic outcomes and is therefore readable as a learned marker. The two pairs, which are never clearly defined as the object of discourse but whose (co)existence is taken for granted, are placed in correlation because Ilya imagines that miatel' has surrendered the -ja-, useless to it, to zaets, who would have preferred it by virtue of the relatability of the form of the -ja-/я to a stylised, albeit earless, rabbit. In return, he would have ceded his -e-: the two forms of the modern standard, zaiats and metel', would thus have been defined by their internal agreement, with extremely poetic and synesthetic characters due to the decisive role played by the graphemes themselves. This language play recalls the ancient Russian setting of the novel, whose plot seems to take place simultaneously long ago and in the years after WWII. Here, Sokolov also alludes to the story of how Alexander Pushkin, the father of Russian letters, encountered a hare on the road while on his way to support the Decembrist Revolt and took it as a bad omen.
ru_trans:
Слово "метель" раньше писалось через "я" ("мятель"), тогда как слово "заяц" писалоьсь через "е" ("заец"). В этом отрывке, как предполагает Мартина Наполитано, Соколов играет с "неотчетливым произношением безударных гласных в русском языке, чреватым неправильным написанием я, е, й" (Napolitano, “Studyin This Volapuke” 289). Буквы передаются от одного слова-образа другому. Здесь Соколов также ссылается на историю о том, как Александр Пушкин, отце русской письменности, встретил зайца по пути на декабристское восстание и принял это за дурное предзнаменование.

Пары метель/мятель и заяц/заец фигурируют  сочетаниями с разными лингвистическими явлениями: метель/мятель отражает альтернативное использование гласной, связанное с орфографической нестабильностью, присутствующей в 19 веке, которой пользовались такие великие писатели как Пушкин и Блок, частично благодаря возможности отражения разных семантических значений (см. Vasil'ev 2008 - VASIL’EV 2008: Vasil’ev S., “Metel’” ili “Mjatel’”? O zaglavii povesti A. S. Puškina, in «Russkaja reč’» 6 (2008), pp. 8-11, http://russkayarech.ru/files/issues/2008/6/02-vasiljev.pdf.). На самом деле, метель происходит от слова "мести" (метлой), тогда как мятель берет начало от глагола "мястить", то есть вызывать смятение, хаос. Авторы, четко различающие оба варианта, безусловно, скорее придают слову "мятель" оттенок смятения, ведь выразительный подтекст слова преобладает над сухой характеристикой природного явления.

text: Ilya uses Biblical wording, taken from [Matthew 7:7](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+7%3A7&version=NIV;NRT): “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you." I always felt that in this list the best books were really missing—clearly the Bible, the New Testament. How much did the authors of the New Testament write? text: Ilya frequently speaks of himself in the third-person. A choice associated with his heavily colloquial speech. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: In the original the word play is between "metel'" (blizzard) and "zayats" (hare). The first one was previously spelled "myatel'," as the second was once spelled "zaets." In this section, as Martina Napolitano suggests, Sokolov plays with "the close pronunciation of certain unaccented vowels in Russian, which often gives rise to misspelling – я, е, й" (“Studyin This Volapuke” 289). Letters are transferred from word/concept to word/concept. The pairs metel'/miatel' and zaits/zaets appear in connection with different linguistic phenomena: metel'/miatel' reflects an alternative use of the vowel linked to the spelling instability still dominant in the nineteenth century and on which many authors, from Pushkin to Blok, played, also because of the possibility to reflect a different semantic intention (see Vasil'ev). Metel', in fact, has its root in the verb mesti, to sweep, while that of miatel' is to be found in the verb miastis', to provoke smiatenie (confusion, disarray); in authors who make conscious and calibrated use of the two variants, it is precisely with this condition that the use of miatel' is to be associated, as its strong expressive connotation prevails over the simple and objective identification of the natural phenomenon. Zaiats-zaets refers to the different outcome of the nasalised -e- of late proto-Slavic, which becomes, in East Slavonic, -ia- and, in South Slavonic, -e-: zaiats is, therefore, the more purely Russian form, while zaets reflects Slavonic-ecclesiastic outcomes and is therefore readable as a learned marker. The two pairs, which are never clearly defined as the object of discourse but whose (co)existence is taken for granted, are placed in correlation because Ilya imagines that miatel' has surrendered the -ja-, useless to it, to zaets, who would have preferred it by virtue of the relatability of the form of the -ja-/я to a stylised, albeit earless, rabbit. In return, he would have ceded his -e-: the two forms of the modern standard, zaiats and metel', would thus have been defined by their internal agreement, with extremely poetic and synesthetic characters due to the decisive role played by the graphemes themselves. This language play recalls the ancient Russian setting of the novel, whose plot seems to take place simultaneously long ago and in the years after WWII. Here, Sokolov also alludes to the story of how Alexander Pushkin, the father of Russian letters, encountered a hare on the road while on his way to support the Decembrist Revolt and took it as a bad omen.

Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Ilya mentions that he once wanted to modify one (R151/E5). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Sokolov explains this passage as follows: "While loading cartridges, the Binging Hunter drinks and gets drunker and drunker, so he starts to think illogically and confuses calibers. He has a 20-caliber smoothbore shotgun, but it seems to him that the cartridges he is loading are 22-caliber. However, he does not see any contradiction in this, on the contrary: it seems to him that everything is in order, that twenty and twenty-two are the same, that such cartridges will fit the shotgun. This logic becomes especially paradoxical when one considers that 22-caliber cartridges are suitable only for rifle shooting, in other words, it is a purely rifled caliber" (personal communication, August 25, 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "Снаряжая патроны, Запойный пьет и пьянеет все больше, поэтому начинает мыслить нелогично и путает калибры. У него гладкоствольное ружье двадцатого калибра, но ему кажется, что снаряжаемые патроны -  двадцать второго калибра. Он, однако, не усматривает в этом противоречия, наоборот: ему кажется, что все в порядке, что двадцать и двадцать два - одно и то же, что такие патроны подойдут к ружью. text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).

Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).
