text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Animal-human motif.

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it will be Krylobyl in chapter 14 who Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise." In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

Это неудивительно, ведь его "говорящее имя" образовано словами "крыло" и "был". text: According to Boguslawski's annotations, *zimar'* refers to Andrei Voznesensky's poem "Song-travesty from the spectacle 'Antiworlds'" (1963) ("Annotations" 233). It combines the word *zima* (winter) with the ending of *ianvar'* (January) to refer to the winter time. Perhaps a reference to the Orion constellation visible during the winter solstice. According to the mythology, Orion fell in love with Merope (along with many other women) and raped her, similar to the story told here by Orina. Constellation-heavens motif.

Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

*В овраге* (*In The Ravine*) — a 1900 novella by Anton Chekhov. Chekhov’s text depicts the end of the patriarchal lifestyle in the Russian country under the pressure of industrialization. With this novella Chekhov moves from intellectual characters to factory workers. An intriguing interpretation was offered by Vladimir Nabokov in his lectures on Russian literature: he believed *In the Ravine* depicted “a world of deception, of mutual cheating” (*Lectures* 310).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: According to Ostanin, a reference to Nikolai Nekrasov's 1846 poem "The Troika": "Всё лицо твоё вспыхнуло вдруг" (32). text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Yakov mentions in Note 2 that the "lonesome babe" chides him for abandoning his boots (R165/E29). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement [...] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his '[Musée des Beaux Arts](http://www.kulichki.com/moshkow/POEZIQ/AUDEN/poems_meerson.txt)'. Running through the images of Brueghel's [*The Census at Bethlehem*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg) (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of *[Landscape with the Fall of Icarus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg)* (ca. 1558)" (*The Prose* 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also [Mario Caramitti’s article “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia.”](https://www.openstarts.units.it/bitstream/10077/2377/1/23.pdf) Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow* derives, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to  a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

Стасова, группа стала эпицентром развития нового национального стиля русской музыки, в основе которого лежали крестьянские традиции и фольклор. Могучая кучка была тесно связана и черпала вдохновение у художественного движения Передвижников …]. Яков намерен передать ту же идею. Он поселяется на Волге, чтобы запечатлить и отобразить жизнь тамошних людей. Помимо поэтического дара, Яков также наделен художественным талантом, и это его работы формируют словесную галерею прозаических глав. "Экспонаты" галереи или графически выделены курсивом, то есть, относятся к названию картины, или определяются отсылкой к "прототипу" образа" (Kravchenko, "The Prose" 61). Одена в его "[Музее изящных искусств". О присутствии и роли образов и подтекстов Брейгеля можно прочитать в статье М. Карамитти "Мультифильмы Брейгеля" (Caramitti, “Mul’tfilmy Breigelia”).

text: The narrator here suggests that it's the circumstances determine a thing's appearance, character, and so on, rather than the other way around. In other words, different contexts will generate different phenomena, much as the characters and settings in the novel shift depending on how their parts and configurations have been arranged around them. In short, a suggestion that art is self-defining.

text: The stress should fall on the last syllable. In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. text: Original Russian: ичиги (*ichigi*). A Tatar light shoe with a soft toe. Also used by peoples of the Caucasus and Central Asia. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: The hoopoe appears several times throughout the novel, mostly in Yakov's poems (R167, 168, 169, 233, 236, 262, 280/E31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 145, 149, 199). José Vergara writes: "the hoopoe plays a key role in the story of Tereus in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. In this myth, the Thracian king rapes Philomela, his wife Procne’s sister, and cuts out her tongue to keep the secret. After Philomela manages to convey to Procne what happened, the sisters conspire to kill the latter’s son, Itys, and feed him to Tereus. Upon learning of their actions, Tereus in turn seeks them out, but before he can enact his revenge, the gods transform them all into birds: Procne into a swallow, Philomela into a nightingale, Tereus into a hoopoe. According to the folklore, the hoopoe’s hooting call is said to mean “where, where” in Greek – Tereus’s plea as he searches for his displaced family" ("Flap" 364–365). Throughout the novel, Ilya is associated with the hoopoe in that he also looks for his missing family. Therefore, Ilya reenacts this plot as he seeks out Orina and their son, Yakov. "He is displaced, like Tereus, in his various transformations and peregrinations, pursuing his idealized family," Vergara continues, "but constantly mired by the imagery he uses and that is used to describe him" ("Flap" 366). Animal-human motif.

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Names for the plants *Euonymus europaens* (European spindle) and *Solanum dulcamara* (bittersweet nightshade). A reflection of the characters' various, shifting names. Gerald Smith compares this passage to the verse of Velimir Khlebnikov (1885–1922) and his literary descendants, including the OBERIU poets ("The Verse" 334). According to S. Efimova: "The words found and invented by the author are mixed: in V.I. Dahl's dictionary there are "beresklet," "brusklet," "beresdren," "bereske," "berendeika," and "bud'derevo"; the writer invented the word "bredovnik," and "brusklet" is modified into "burusklen." While working as a huntsman, who provided the material for the novel, the writer was greatly influenced by the speech of local residents. The selection of consonant words from folk dialects also allowed him to convey a fabulous, folkloric picture of the world, as well as the first group of metaphors" (43). Plant motif.

The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Yakov mentions in Note 2 that the "lonesome babe" chides him for abandoning his boots (R165/E29). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

Olga Matich writes of the sewing themes: "Yet the verb “weave” and noun “weaving” appear only rarely in the novel
and only with its meaning defamiliarized or rewoven, for example in the wellknown colloquial idiom in which weaving words is a metaphor for speaking nonsense ('Ой, плетете вы сами не знаете что,' 142), perhaps intended as
a parody of word-weaving. Another estranged usage is that of '*pleten'*' (wattle fence) metamorphosed into a thrice removed distant relative ('троюродный плетень,' 112); or '*spletni*' (108), meaning gossip, which comes from the verb 'spletat’' (weave in the sense of intertwine). The altercation between Ilya
and the wolf on the ice inscribes reweaving (*perepletat*) rendered as 'Мудрено индивиду в таких переплетах баланс удерживать' (139) [...] '*Pereplet*' means book binding, with its plural in this passage metaphorized as a situation in which Ilya finds it difficult to keep his balance on the ice. The phrase, I would suggest, may also be a nod to *Between Dog and Wolf*’s readers who sometimes find it very difficult to interpret that which they encounter between its, so to speak, woven, rewoven, or interwoven 'bindings'" (*Between Dog and Wolf* 255–256).

text: A central motif in the novel, this phrase alludes to *The Hunters in the Snow*, a 1565 painting by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. The setting and action of this image recurs throughout *Between Dog and Wolf* (e.g., R202–203/E93–95), as they come to life in the text. Elena Kravchenko explains: "Besides the 'trope' of the exhibition viewing, the device of ekphrasis, and the 'gallery' structure of The Pictures, Sokolov borrows the underlying 'teleology' of Musorgskii’s work. Alongside Borodin, Balakirev, Cui, and Rimskii Korsakov, Musorgskii was one of the 'Mighty Handful' ('Moguchaia kuchka'). Created under the patronage of an art critic Vladimir Stasov, it became the hub of a pioneering national style which espoused folklore and the traditions of the peasantry as the new foundation for Russian music. The group was closely connected with and drew inspiration from the Wanderers, an artistic movement […] Iakov is set to communicate a similar idea. He comes to the Volga to grasp and represent the lives of its people. Besides his poetic gift, Iakov is an artist, and it is his works that form the textual gallery of the prose chapters. The gallery 'entries' are either demarcated graphically with italics, which signals a title of a painting, or framed by a reference to their pictorial 'origin'" (*The Prose* 61). She continues: "It can be argued that Iakov’s representation of human suffering, which constitutes one of the main themes of the novel, and which has been identified as the major moral message of many Brueghel paintings, is modelled not directly on Brueghel but on W. H. Auden's ekphrasis in his 'Musée des Beaux Arts'. Running through the images of Brueghel's *[The Census at Bethlehem](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Census_at_Bethlehem_-_WGA03379.jpg)* (1566) and *[The Slaughter of the Innocents](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_the_Innocents_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)* (ca. 1564), it culminates in the ekphrasis of [*Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Pieter_Bruegel_de_Oude_-_De_val_van_Icarus.jpg) (ca. 1558)" (The Prose 63). On the presence and role of Bruegel’s imagery and subtext, see also Mario Caramitti’s article “[Mul’tfilmy Breigelia](https://www.openstarts.units.it/server/api/core/bitstreams/91ab62b1-20af-4e0c-ba32-e45c7baeaf2d/content).” Beyond these obvious ekphrastic connections between Sokolov’s novel and Bruegel’s painting, these are other points worth noting. For instance, the series from which *Hunters in the Snow derives*, *The Seasons* (1565) is divided into six paintings, five of which remain extant. “If a division of the year into six pictures seems strange initially,” Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “this proves to have been a common way of diving the annual cycle in the Netherlands during the period, as early spring and spring and early summer and midsummer were differentiated. The year’s inherently cyclic character relativizes the discussion around the ‘correct’ order of the pictures – which painting represents the beginning and which the end of the series” (214). Much the same may be said about the structure of *Between Dog and Wolf*, in which the poetic chapters trace the development of seasonal changes, while everything exists in an in-between state (seasons, characters’ identities, etc.). It is also worth noting that, as in Sokolov’s text where strict adherence to geographical reality is not observed, the landscapes depicted in the *Seasons* paintings are not accurate: “These so-called ‘mixed landscapes’ combine memories of the Alps with typically Flemish motifs” (229). There is something to be said about the way Sokolov, like Bruegel develops a “sheer inexhaustible richness of detail” that inevitably leads to “the limits of visual perception and linguistic representation” (215). One particular detail of the painting, apparently not described by Sokolov in the novel, feels relevant: “Thick icicles have claimed the mill wheel at the right edge and brought it to a halt, as though time itself has frozen” (228). Indeed, time and therefore the characters feel stuck in the world of *Between Dog and Wolf*.

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: According to D. Barton Johnson, this was the first poem written by Sokolov for the novel. It was written in July 1976 on a train between Zürich and Locarno ("Background Notes" 338). Indeed, in a letter dated March 3, 1981, wrote the following to his friend and critic: "I had a premonition of the book, a forefeeling—the general contours, an outline, if you will. The poems appeared on their own. I wrote the first poem on a train, on the way from Zürich to Locarno, in July 76. That was Note IX, which parodies Pushkin's style. It seems to have been successful, although in Sov[iet] criticism there's a widespread opinion that it's impossible to parody Pushkin, because it's like parodying the Russian language itself" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections). Railroad theme.
ru_trans: По словам Д. Бартона Джонсона, это было первое стихотворение, написанное Соколовым для романа. Оно было написано в июле 1976 года в поезде между Цюрихом и Локарно (Johnson, "Background Notes" 338). Действительно, в письме от 3 марта 1981 года Соколов написал следующее своему другу и критику: "У меня было предчувствие книги, предощущение — и общий контур, абрис, если угодно. Стихи появились сами. Первое стихотворение написал в поезде, по дороге из Цюриха в Локарно, в июле 76 года. Это была Записка IX, пародирующая пушкинский стиль. Кажется, удалась, хотя в сов[етской] критике распространено мнение, что Пушкина пародировать невозможно, ибо это все равно, что пародировать сам русский язык" (Box 12, Folder 5, Don Johnson Papers, UC Santa Barbara Special Research Collections). text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. [...] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: From the French "*cerceau*." Hoop rolling — a children's game in which hoops are kept rolling with a stick or other device. Depicted in the bottom center of the 1560 painting *Children's Games* by Bruegel: Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “*Children’s Games* is one of the earliest known panel paintings by Bruegel. […] Bruegel’s encyclopaedic approach is not limited to the depiction of the greatest possible variety of games but also embraces the rendering of a whole gamut of personal dispositions, from calm to aggressive. With just a few strokes of the brush the painter manages to give each of the protagonists a clearly legible expression that goes well beyond stock characterization, through the play of facial features and body language. Different types of customs make it clear that Bruegel was intending to depict a miscellany of children's activities from all four seasons” (132). Ostanin also notes that Серко (Serko) is the name given to dogs in the Ukrainian fairy tale "Серко" (33).
ru_trans: От французского cerceau. Детская игра в обруч, при которой движение обруча поддерживается палкой или другим предметом. Изображено внизу в центре картины Брейгеля 1560 года "Детские игры". С. Пено и Э. Оберталер пишут: "'Детские игры' — одно из самых ранних известных панельных картин Брейгеля. […] Энциклопедический подход Брейгеля не ограничивается изображением максимально возможного разнообразия игр — он также охватывает всю гамму личных настроений, от спокойных до агрессивных. Всего лишь несколькими взмахами кисти художнику удается придать каждому герою ясно читаемое выражение, выходящее далеко за рамки стандартной характеристики за счет обыгранных выражения лица и языка тела. Различные виды обычаев дают понять, что Брейгель намеревался изобразить мизансцену детских забав всех четырех времен года" (132). Останин также замечает, что Серко — собачье имя из украинской сказки "Серко" (33).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

A reference to Pushkin's nanny, Arina Rodionovna Yakovleva (1758–1828). Pushkin retained a loving attitude to her, even dedicating poems to her and taking notes from her folk tales and tunes; she opened up for him an entire peasant world in terms of motifs, characters, and even words. Tatyana’s nanny from his masterpiece *Eugene Onegin* draws on her profile. Tatyana thrice says "Ах, няня..." (ch. 3, stanzas 19, 34, 35). Also mentioned in Note XXV (R234/E146).
ru_trans: Отсылка к няне Пушкина, Арине Родионовне Яковлевой (1758–1828). Ей посвящено несколько произведений Пушкина. Пушкин сохранил к ней теплую привязанность, посвящая ей даже стихи и записывая ее народные сказки и напевы; она открыла ему целый крестьянский мир в плане мотивов, персонажей и даже слов. В романе в стихах Пушкина *Евгений Онегин*, главная героиня Татьяна трижды повторяет: "Ах, няня…" (гл. 3, строфы 19, 34, 35). Также упоминается в Записке XXV (R234/E146).

text: Mentioned four times in the novel with different surnames (R153/E7, R199/E89, R242/E161, R278/E225). The name of Arabic origin Aladdin (Al al-Din) means “nobility of faith” and was popularized by the success of *One Thousand and One Nights*, before the 1992 homonymous Disney movie. Here it is used to suggest the Tatar origin of the character (directly indicated in Note XIV). His last name is mentioned alternatively as Batrutdinov and Rakhmatullin: the first derives from the Arabic name Batrutdin which means “full moon of the faith”; the second is a Tatar or Bashkir last name, derived from the name Rahmatullah, “mercy of God.”
ru_trans: Четырежды упоминается в романе под разными фамилиями (R153/E7, R199/E89, R242/E161, R278/E225). Алладин — имя арабского происхождения (Ала́ ад-Дин) означает "благородство веры" и стало известным благодаря успеху "Тысячи и одной ночи" ещё до выхода одноимённого Диснеевского мультифильма в 1992. Здесь оно используется как намек на татарское происхождение героя (прямо раскрывается в Записке 15). Фамилия упоминается или как Батурдинов, или как Рахматуллин: первая происходит от арабского имени Батрудин, означающего "полнолуние верности"; вторая — татаро-башкирская фамилия, произошедшая от имени Рахматулла, "милость Божья". text: Sokolov explains: "This is an ordinary village well with a windlass. The bucket is lowered and lifted with the aid of a windlass and a rope wrapped around it. From time to time in some village someone falls into the well wanting to draw water. Sometimes a child, sometimes a drunken adult. Sometimes a dog or a cat. If there is water in the well, the victim drowns. But if the well is dry, there is a chance that sooner or later the person or animal will be pulled out. They will if people hear screams or meows for help. It is impossible to get out of the well by yourself. The huntsman Ilya tells us about most likely fell into the well, as they say, because he was drunk, and his wife hastened to take advantage of this circumstance. There is nothing allegorical in the fall of the huntsman into the well" (personal communication, June 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "Имеется в виду обычный деревенский колодец с воротом. С помощью ворота и намотанной на него веревки осуществляют спуск и подъем ведра. Время от времени то в той деревне, то в этой кто-нибудь, желая зачерпнуть воды, падает в колодец. Иногда ребенок, иногда пьяный взрослый. Подчас собака или кошка. Если в колодце есть вода, жертва тонет. А если колодец сухой, то есть шанс, что рано или поздно человека или животное вытащат оттуда. Вытащат, если услышат крики или мяуканья о помощи. Самому выбраться из колодца невозможно. Егерь, о котором рассказывает Илья, скорее всего угодил в колодец, как говорится, по пьяному делу, и жена его этим обстоятельством поспешила воспользоваться. В падении егеря в колодец нет ничего иносказательного" (личное сообщение, 7 июня 2023).

text: The mythical Firebird from Slavic folklore. Read the original [here](https://xn----7sbb5adknde1cb0dyd.xn--p1ai/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/) and an English translation [here](http://www.artrusse.ca/fairytales/firebird.htm). In one version of the story, the Firebird transforms into a crow (as mentioned at the end of this sentence). Margaret Ziolkowski explains: "The bird resumes its fantastic form when Ivan returns safely home. Ivan's father wonders what this transformation signifies, and the answer seems to be that the Firebird's temporary metamorphosis into a dreary-looking crow is a symbolic consequence of Ivan's betrayal by his brothers [...] In Sokolov's novel, many primarily sexual betrayals occur, but also a more wide-ranging metaphysical betrayal. The world portrayed in *Between Dog and Wolf* is marred by spiritual emptiness and pervasive cynicism, and the reference to the Firebird belies the loveliness of the landscape. The Firebird's sad transformation is symbolically akin to the many images of physical and psychological maiming that occur in all three of Sokolov's novels and point to the fractured and fragmented nature of existence" (414). Animal motif.

Прочитать сказку о ней можно [здесь](https://онлайн-читать.рф/%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%B6%D0%B0%D1%80-%D0%BF%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%86%D0%B0/). История разворачивается в царстве, где неизвестный крадет яблоки из королевского сада. Трем принцам нужно найти вора. Младший, Иван-царевич, замечает, что дивная Жар-птица крадет яблоки, но ему удается поймать лишь пару ее перьев. Король изумляется их красотой и поручает сыновьям захватить Жар-птицу, в чем, в конце концов, преуспеет лишь Иван-царевич. Однако на пути назад он решает отдохнуть, и, преисполненные завистью, братья решают убить его. С помощью друга-волка у Ивана-царевича удается вернуться и восстановить порядок в царстве. text: A Nikolai different from Nikolai the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Другой Николай, не относящийся к Николаю Угоднику, описанному выше. Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text:
Olga Matich writes of the sewing themes: "Yet the verb “weave” and noun “weaving” appear only rarely in the novel
and only with its meaning defamiliarized or rewoven, for example in the wellknown colloquial idiom in which weaving words is a metaphor for speaking nonsense ('Ой, плетете вы сами не знаете что,' 142), perhaps intended as
a parody of word-weaving. Another estranged usage is that of '*pleten'*' (wattle fence) metamorphosed into a thrice removed distant relative ('троюродный плетень,' 112); or '*spletni*' (108), meaning gossip, which comes from the verb 'spletat’' (weave in the sense of intertwine). The altercation between Ilya
and the wolf on the ice inscribes reweaving (*perepletat*) rendered as 'Мудрено индивиду в таких переплетах баланс удерживать' (139) [...] '*Pereplet*' means book binding, with its plural in this passage metaphorized as a situation in which Ilya finds it difficult to keep his balance on the ice. The phrase, I would suggest, may also be a nod to *Between Dog and Wolf*’s readers who sometimes find it very difficult to interpret that which they encounter between its, so to speak, woven, rewoven, or interwoven 'bindings'" (*Between Dog and Wolf* 255–256).

And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Death. The reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Nikolai's name shortens to Nikola. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

text: From the French "*cerceau*." Hoop rolling — a children's game in which hoops are kept rolling with a stick or other device. Depicted in the bottom center of the 1560 painting *Children's Games* by Bruegel: Sabine Pénot and Elke Oberthaler write, “*Children’s Games* is one of the earliest known panel paintings by Bruegel. […] Bruegel’s encyclopaedic approach is not limited to the depiction of the greatest possible variety of games but also embraces the rendering of a whole gamut of personal dispositions, from calm to aggressive. With just a few strokes of the brush the painter manages to give each of the protagonists a clearly legible expression that goes well beyond stock characterization, through the play of facial features and body language. Different types of customs make it clear that Bruegel was intending to depict a miscellany of children's activities from all four seasons” (132). Ostanin also notes that Серко (Serko) is the name given to dogs in the Ukrainian fairy tale "Серко" (33).
