text: Ilya's conversation with the river here is continued in chapter 4 (R176/E47-48). There, the "Страшнеющего Суда" becomes "последнем случае." The threat of death and the pull of suicide looms over Ilya and many of the men living on the banks of the Volga. However, as Martina Napolitano explains, "As if to exorcise it, as if to disavow it as incompatible with the characters' very personal idea of a-chronological, nonlinear, circular and modifiable time, death is always spoken of in a metaphorical key" ("'Studyin This Volapuke'" 287). Death is one of Sokolov's central themes. As he put it in an interview with Olga Matich, "In that sense, I'm apparently traditional. I write on eternal themes: love, life, death. Death is inseparable from life. It's constantly near, around us, in the objects that surround us. It becomes clearer in certain of its forms. For example, in old photographs. Since I was a child I've had a thought: everyone in photos from the previous century, at the very least those born in its first half, died. This fact particularly stands out when you look at group photos, at snapshots of massive street scenes. Or when you're simply walking down the street at rush hour and suddenly see a freeze frame. All movement, the entire crowd momentarily stops, and you suddenly remember: in 60-70 years all of them will no longer be. Yourself included" ("Nuzhno zabyt'" 12). This fascination with death dates back to his childhood: "Visiting cemeteries [...] was for me something like a home education. I was also interested in the theme of death. It's, after all, the most interesting thing in life" (Kochetkova).
ru_trans: Разговор Ильи с рекой продолжается в главе 4 (R176/E47-48). Здесь, выражение "до Страшнеющего Суда" становится синонимичным "в последнем случае". Угроза смерти и тяга к самоубийству давлеет над Ильей и другими обитателями берегов Волги. Однако, как объясняет М. Наполитано: "Будто бы бы для того, чтобы освободиться, отречься от нее как от идеи, несовместимой с весьма личным ахронологическим, нелинейным, спиралевидным, легкоизменяемым понятием времени героев, о смерти всегда говорится в метафорическом ключе" (Napolitano, "'Studyin This Volapuke'" 287). Смерть является одной из центральных тем в творчестве Соколова. Как он замечает в интервью с Ольгой Матич: "В этом смысле я, видимо, традиционен. Пишу на вечные темы: любовь, жизнь, смерть. Смерть неотлучима от жизни. Она постоянно рядом, вокруг нас, в окружающих нас предметах. В некоторых из них ее облик проступает ясней. Например, в старых фотографиях. Меня с детства занимала мысль: все люди на снимках прошлого века, во всяком случае — родившиеся в первой половине его, умерли. Особенно этот факт поражает при взгляде на групповые фото, на снимки массовых уличных сцен. Или просто идешь по улице в часы пик и вдруг видишь как бы стоп-кадр: все движение, вся толпа мгновенно останавливается и вспоминаешь вдруг: через 60-70 лет их всех тоже не будет. И тебя в том числе" (Solokov, "Nuzhno zabyt'" 12). Увлечение темой смерти зародилось еще в детстве: "Посещение кладбищ — не только Ваганьковского, но и Симоновского и Новодевичьего — было для меня чем-то вроде домашнего образования. Меня тоже интересовала тема смерти — это ведь самое интересное, что есть в жизни" (Kochetkova).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). text: Ilya's struggle with his footwear echoes that of Cinderella. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).

text: Diminutive of Ilya. Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

Another spelling of Gorodnishche. The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (*gorod*) and beggar (*nishchii*). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Ilya's conversation with the river here is continued in chapter 4 (R176/E47-48). There, the "Lastest Judgment" becomes "the latter case." The threat of death and the pull of suicide looms over Ilya and many of the men living on the banks of the Volga. However, as Martina Napolitano explains, "As if to exorcise it, as if to disavow it as incompatible with the characters' very personal idea of a-chronological, nonlinear, circular and modifiable time, death is always spoken of in a metaphorical key" ("'Studyin This Volapuke'" 287). Death is one of Sokolov's central themes. As he put it in an interview with Olga Matich, "In that sense, I'm apparently traditional. I write on eternal themes: love, life, death. Death is inseparable from life. It's constantly near, around us, in the objects that surround us. It becomes clearer in certain of its forms. For example, in old photographs. Since I was a child I've had a thought: everyone in photos from the previous century, at the very least those born in its first half, died. This fact particularly stands out when you look at group photos, at snapshots of massive street scenes. Or when you're simply walking down the street at rush hour and suddenly see a freeze frame. All movement, the entire crowd momentarily stops, and you suddenly remember: in 60-70 years all of them will no longer be. Yourself included" ("Nuzhno zabyt'" 12). This fascination with death dates back to his childhood: "Visiting cemeteries [...] was for me something like a home education. I was also interested in the theme of death. It's, after all, the most interesting thing in life" (Kochetkova).
